segments.input: Take a collection of random points and divide their labels into two groups. Imagine stretching a rubber sheet around each group. How likely are the two enclosed shapes to intersect? This AI-assisted, unrefereed mathematical candidate studies points sampled independently from the same Gaussian distribution. It asks how the intersection probability changes as the groups become more balanced. A published theorem answers the question for dimension plus two points. This paper adds one point: dimension plus three. The probabilities are log-concave, a precise inequality that implies they rise towards the centre and then fall symmetrically. The reason is geometric. Whenever a labelled split has intersecting convex hulls, exactly two points can be deleted while preserving that intersection.

segments.input: Averaging this identity connects the larger sample to the already understood smaller one. Four points on a line give a concrete example. For a fixed one-versus-three split, the intersection probability is one half. For a fixed two-versus-two split, it is two thirds. These are probabilities for fixed labels, not the distribution of a randomly chosen partition size. The paper also identifies an explicit margin in the log-concavity inequality and precise local equality conditions. The general arrangement identities and qualitative convolution theorem are established background, not new claims. The scope remains narrow. The argument does not settle the cases with dimension plus four or more points, and does not rule out every wider central plateau.
